Datadog surged 6% to $273, nearing its $293 52-week high, but a trailing P/E of 504x leaves little room for any execution stumble.

Dynatrace slipped 0.8% and the software ETF (IGV) fell while Datadog rallied, signaling targeted conviction buying in one name over the broader sector.

Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG) stock is up 6% to $272.50, a sharp gain for the observability and monitoring company. That strength arrives against a weaker software group, giving Datadog stock a move that belongs to it alone.

Mobile software development lab by itcollege.ee / BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/)

Across software, the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (NYSEARCA:IGV) is down 0.4%, which puts Datadog stock on the opposite side of its own sector. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.5%, so the broad market is slightly higher while software lags behind it.

At the same time, Dynatrace (NYSE:DT) stock is down 0.8% to $58.23, a mild slip for the company Datadog competes with most directly in observability. Taken together, those three readings describe a single-stock rally, with Datadog stock carrying the move on its own shoulders.

Datadog Moves Apart From Software

Datadog stock is climbing while Dynatrace stock and the software fund are both falling, a split that points to buying aimed squarely at this one name, and a gain of this size traces back to demand for Datadog specifically when a software fund slips and a direct observability competitor slides alongside it.

Isolated strength in Datadog stock can reflect conviction in the platform's long-run staying power, since buyers are paying up for one monitoring provider while passing on Dynatrace stock. Such concentrated rallies can also fade once enthusiasm cools off, which is why the valuation behind Datadog stock deserves a closer look.

Checking in on some of Datadog's other peers, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock is down 0.77% to $138.46. Meanwhile, Cloudflare (NYSE:NET) stock is slipping 2% to $350.77.

title: Fastly’s 14% AI spike was a mirage; Here’s the edge stock Citi says you should own
detail:
Fastly’s 14% AI spike was a mirage; Here’s the edge stock Citi says you should own
Louis Juricic

FSLY
NET
META

Investing.com -- Fastly (NYSE: FSLY) saw its stock drop 9% on Thursday, wiping out some of the 14% surge it enjoyed on Wednesday. The earlier spike was fueled by new data showing Fastly plays a major role in powering Meta's new AI assistant, Muse. However, Citi analyst Fatima Boolani isn't buying the hype and remains neutral on the stock.

Still guessing which names to buy? Our AI rebuilds its stock picks at the start of every month. The list is beating the market by 120%. See what's on it »

In a research note published Thursday, Boolani argued that the bump in traffic from Meta's AI won't automatically lead to the kind of massive profits needed to justify Fastly's recent stock rally. Instead, she prefers Cloudflare (NYSE: NET) as the best way to invest in this type of AI infrastructure. Even though Cloudflare's stock is much more expensive, Boolani believes the premium is worth it because the company has a proven track record of actually making money from these new technologies.

The excitement around Fastly started when a Yahoo Finance report highlighted that the company handles a surprisingly large chunk of the web traffic generated by Meta's Muse. Fastly had hinted at this partnership during an investor event the day before, noting that popular AI assistants were starting to drive massive amounts of traffic across its network. Citi also pointed out that Fastly already counts six of the world's seven largest tech companies as customers.

The problem, according to Citi, is how Fastly charges for this specific type of AI traffic. AI assistants send lots of tiny, quick requests back and forth, rather than large, heavy files like streaming video. Because Fastly charges customers based on the total amount of data transferred (per gigabyte) rather than the number of requests made, it isn't making as much money on these lightweight AI interactions. If Fastly charged per request, profits would be much higher, but there's no sign they are doing that yet.

Boolani also pointed out that Fastly seems to be providing basic, low-profit data delivery for Meta. Fastly makes its real money by selling advanced security features, like protecting websites from bots and hackers. So far, there's little evidence that Meta is buying these extra, high-profit security services alongside the basic traffic delivery. While the AI storyline sounds great, Citi needs to see Fastly actually selling these add-ons before getting excited.
